summary:
Greenland stands under Denmark's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here. It is a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark, with its own parliament and courts for domestic law, while criminal law and official document rules remain Danish.

Same-sex relations are lawful, and the territory's record on partnership and marriage has been permissive for three decades. Partnership law was adopted from the Danish model in 1996 and passed with virtually no debate, and it has since been replaced by the marriage law.

Same-sex marriage came into effect in April 2016. Greenland adopted Danish legislation that had passed unanimously twice in Denmark, the first bill lapsing after Danish elections, and the local parliament enacted it without recorded opposition; it replaced the 1996 partnership law. The bishop of the established church supported it.

From 2016 Greenland has used a self-declaration approach to gender recognition, an approach adopted ahead of Denmark's own practice.

The social picture for a visitor is low-friction. Gay life is described as "almost a non-event": low-key, integrated and non-violent, with a modest Pride march since 2010. Organising is present but small in scale, and there is no record in this inventory of organised hostility toward LGBT people.

In August 2014 a new national association, LGBT Qaamaneq, was founded for lesbians, gays, bisexuals and transgender people, pursuing political, cultural and social equality and open to family, friends and colleagues as supporters as well as to its members.

The practical counterweight is capacity rather than hostility. Some 56,000 people live across remote settlements, and specialist services are limited. A trans visitor is unlikely to meet legal obstruction and is more likely to meet limited provision, limited staff, and long distances to the next service point.
tangentialFactors:
Greenland legislates these matters locally but drew its instruments from Denmark. The 2016 marriage law adopted Danish legislation that had passed the Danish parliament unanimously twice, the first bill lapsing after Danish elections, which means the Danish legislative process ran alongside the local one rather than replacing it. The lapse of the first bill is procedural rather than social: there is no record of rejection of same-sex marriage in Greenland itself.

The territory's own law has at times been less demanding than the parent framework. The self-declaration approach to gender recognition adopted from 2016 preceded Denmark's own practice on the same question, so a trans person dealing with Greenland's authorities faces a lighter procedure than the one their Danish counterparts encountered.

The institutional climate carries no recorded opposition. The bishop of the established church publicly supported the 2016 marriage legislation, and Greenlandic Broadcasting carried the founding of a national LGBT association in August 2014 without any sign of controversy. Public visibility here is uncontentious rather than hidden.

Organising remains modest in scale, which matters for a territory of roughly 56,000 people. Pride has been held annually since 2010 as a small march, and LGBT Qaamaneq, founded in 2014, is described as a national association serving lesbians, gays, bisexuals and transgender people and open to supporters outside its membership. For a visitor, this means a visible but thin infrastructure: people are reachable, but there are few of them.

Inatsisartut, the Greenlandic parliament, legislates domestic law including partnership and marriage. The 1996 partnership law was replaced by the marriage law that took effect in April 2016, enacted from Danish legislation that had passed unanimously twice, the first bill lapsing after Danish elections.

Gender recognition in Greenland has used a self-declaration approach since 2016, adopted ahead of Denmark's own practice on the same question.

LGBT Qaamaneq was founded in August 2014 as a national association for lesbians, gays, bisexuals and transgender people, working toward political, cultural and social equality. It is open to family, friends and colleagues as supporters, not only to members.

A modest Pride march has been held since 2010, and LGBT life in Greenland is described in the record as low-key, integrated and non-violent.

outOfScopeNotes:
Gender recognition procedure is only described in this record at the level of principle. The inventory does not document the administrative steps, the authority handling applications, name and marker change rules, or any medical or psychological prerequisites. That description remains unresolved by the sources here.

Nothing in the inventory addresses whether Danish hate-crime or hate-speech provisions extend to Greenland, or whether any local instrument protects gender identity from hostile acts. The non-violence characterisation rests on a 2015 cultural and travel account rather than an official or academic assessment.

No source covers entry, visa or border-screening practice for trans travellers, document-check experience, or the treatment of gender markers at ports of entry.

Facilities, prison placement, gendered accommodation and access to gender-affirming healthcare are not addressed. The only scale information available is the population of roughly 56,000 across remote settlements, which implies thin services but does not establish what those services are.

The single source on LGBT Qaamaneq dates from 2014. Its current activity, membership, funding and remit are not sourced here.
